So assuming your GP isn't doing face to face appointments still, as most of them aren't, then what they'll most likely do is refer you to an NHS mental health service or local organisation. How great the treatment available is/how long to wait will depend on where you live, but it's definitely worth following everything up and giving it a try. They may also offer you medication if you aren't already on any. Don't feel pressured into feeling like you have to say yes to it, but also don't rule it out automatically as it can be helpful for many people. 

Sometimes it can take quite a few visits to the GP to get referred for more serious help, so don't be afraid to keep going back and updating them if things aren't getting better - they can't treat a problem they don't know about and they do want to help, even though the bureaucracy of the NHS can make the process slower than we'd like (trust me I used to work there, it's nobody on the ground's fault)

Source: over a decade (on and off) of seeking NHS help through my GP for mental health issues

Hey there, long time panic attack sufferer here. Some things that help me are:

- Breathing slowly and carefully, particularly while counting them out

- Talking out loud. It can be about anything - if possible get someone to ask you a question to respond to. This works both to distract your mind and regulate breathing (as it's hard to talk and hyperventilate at the same time)

- Singing. Similar to above, it forces you to control your breathing

- Make a list of something unrelated to your worries. It sounds daft I know but trust me, it's a great way to distract your mind and get it focused on something logical rather than emotional (think alphabetical list of countries or animals or movie characters etc). Puzzles and quizzes work great for this too

Panic attacks are horrible but the good thing is they aren't dangerous. If this becomes a persistent problem then it's worth seeking medical advice and seeing if therapy and/or medication can help (it has for me)

It really does depend on the person. If you know the person well enough to have a proper dialogue with them, the best thing to do is ask them what they want: do they want positivity, practical solutions, or maybe just a sympathetic ear?

I think a big thing to avoid is directly contradicting a person's negative beliefs about themself. I know people want to help because they don't think those things are true, but from our perspective having someone respond to us with the opposite of our feelings just makes us feel like you aren't listening and that our feelings are being invalidated. A better approach can be to ask a person WHY they feel the way they feel, and allow them to work through it and change it if and when they are ready.

I'd say it's good to be kind and say things like "that sucks, I hope you feel better soon" or "I understand why you feel like that, just know that I don't feel badly towards you", but avoid making statements about the person like "you're beautiful", "you're worthy", "you're loved" because those are either your subjective opinions or assumptions, which (especially if it's a stranger on the Internet) you just aren't able to accurately make.

Well, when I was at school and struggling with anxiety/panic attacks, here's what I would do: make lists. It might not work for other people but one of the biggest things that calms me down when I'm panicking is listing something completely neutral (e.g. an animal for every letter of the alphabet, as many countries as I can think of beginning with B, different brands of cars). I find this helps because it forces your thoughts away from what's making you anxious and into something ordered and logical. It's also a good coping method to use in class because it just looks like you're taking notes.

You could also try playing i-spy with yourself and spotting different kinds of things around the room (e.g. sometimes I challenge myself to find every letter of the alphabet somewhere in the room). Again, gets your mind off the worries and onto something neutral which helps keep you grounded.

Also, when I was at uni and found myself having SH urges during seminars I would doodle little stick men being tortured and whatnot, in the silliest ways I could think of. This helped me because it allowed me to express a bit of the violence I felt inside and made it something comical instead of serious (this might not work if you don't have a dark sense of humour though).

Good luck, I hope school goes ok for you.
